-3QPTopWbhQ.title: Founder-led Sales to GTM Team | AJ Tennant (Tenacity Capital)
-3QPTopWbhQ.label: Slush
-3QPTopWbhQ.description:
Most founders hit a wall when it's time to move beyond founder-led sales. Get it wrong and growth stalls or the wrong team gets hired.

AJ Tennant, Founder & GP at Tenacity Capital and former GTM leader at Facebook, Slack, and Glean, knows how to get it right. In this session, he shares how to spot the right moment to hire, build a sales motion that actually works, and avoid the mistakes that kill momentum.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Lead with the why: anchor sales in mission/pain, not features.
- Drive discovery: target ~50/50 talk time; be curious, teach with a POV (Challenger).
- Qualify hard: shift POC/pilot to “Proof of Value” with upfront success criteria and commercial commitment; use give/get.
- Win the people: identify/test the Economic Buyer and a true Champion (e.g., texting relationship, influence).
- Build GTM muscle: set net-new meeting targets, implement CRM/forecast cadence early, add SDRs ~$3M ARR, hire Head of Sales around $5–10M ARR.

—

-jh8flX9Wig.title: Dmitry Gurski: Founder & CEO @Flo Health, Breaking Taboos, Building Trust w/ 70M Users | Slush 2024
-jh8flX9Wig.label: Slush
-jh8flX9Wig.description:
Medical research has historically been biased against women. Before the 1990s, women were rarely included in clinical trials, leading to fatal data gaps in medicine. Many medical conditions affecting uniquely women were left in the shadows, which is evident still today. There are five times as many papers on ResearchGate discussing erectile dysfunction—a condition that affects 19% of men—than on premenstrual syndrome, which affects 90% of women.

The fact that history has been silent on women has meant that women’s health as an industry is full of untapped potential. Yet investors have been slow to get on board—women’s health has remained severely underfunded. What can we learn from building in the space? How do you scale a company in a market that is traditionally perceived as niche and suffers from a chronic lack of investor support? Dmitry Gurski is the perfect person to consult on the topic. His company Flo Health has 60 million monthly active users and over 250 million downloads worldview. In February 2024, it became the first femtech unicorn in Europe.

2wkJH311eaw.label: Slush
2wkJH311eaw.description:
AI is changing how products are built, and so should the teams building them. This session breaks down what AI-native teams look like. What roles you need. How workflows shift. And how to hire for what’s coming next.

Emma Burrows is the Co-founder & CTO of Portia AI and a former engineering leader at Google and Stripe. She’s rethinking how teams should operate in the AI era. With deep experience across infrastructure, product, and leadership, Emma brings hard-earned insight into what it takes to hire, structure, and scale truly AI-native teams.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- AI-native teams change workflows, roles, and shipping to let agents handle large chunks of work, not just tab-completion.
- Shift from line-by-line coding to architecture-level “vibe engineering”: specify the what and the how; agents draft, humans guide and review at the end.
- CLI-based coding agents correlate with deeper AI-native practices than editor-first tools like Cursor.
- Work in thin vertical slices: prompt → agent draft → test/QA → minimal review → iterate.
- Maximize parallelization: keep agents busy and write the next prompt while code is generating to preserve context and speed.

4b3b0lkW7es.description:
early-stage founders don’t need a massive budget to build a brand. this session explores how community-led growth, building in public, and founder personality can drive breakout attention from the first handful of users through to unicorn and beyond.

james hawkins, co-ceo at posthog, has turned a developer tool into a beloved brand with 245,000 customers and a hedgehog at its heart. he shares what works, what doesn’t, and why even serious software should be a little fun.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Community is the moat: in commoditized software, loyal users drive early adoption, feedback, and word-of-mouth growth
- Ship fast, iterate faster: launch before perfect; a forgiving community enables rapid improvement to parity and beyond
- Stand out or get lost: with AI lowering build barriers, brand, personality, and distinct choices across all touchpoints matter
- Be long-term greedy: prioritize user trust (transparent pricing, generous refunds, helpful UX) over short-term extraction
- Go ultra-specific: define a hyper-narrow ICP/persona and build a remarkable experience that may alienate non-target users

Your first funding round can set the tone for your entire company. But most founders only go through it once, and the stakes couldn’t be higher.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Traction outweighs everything in early fundraising; show real customer demand
- Use bottoms-up market sizing (customers × revenue per customer), not just top-down TAM
- Seed investors look for massive markets (~$40B+) or a clear path to expand into them
- Pre-seed is about team, not traction; wrong investor if they demand metrics at this stage
- VCs assess teams on execution, customer/market insight, and character over multiple touchpoints

AI-generated key takeaways
- Prioritize firsthand experience over interviews to find real startup ideas; avoid “LARPing.”

- Use the Pull Framework: urgent project, poor current options, clear fit, and buy without persuasion.

- Build one repeatable case study; iterate recordings/notes to improve fit and scale by repeating it.

7f1EE_zdrfU.title: Choosing The Right Funding | Marcus Räder (Hostaway)
7f1EE_zdrfU.label: Slush
7f1EE_zdrfU.description:
The funding path you choose will shape everything. It affects your product, your speed, your team, and your outcome. But most founders do not truly understand the tradeoffs until they are deep into the journey. This session breaks down the real differences between bootstrapping, venture capital, and private equity.

Marcus Rader is the Founder and CEO of Hostaway. He bootstrapped the company from the ground up and scaled it into Europe’s leading short-term rental platform. In 2024, he closed a 350 million euro private equity round that made Hostaway the first unicorn in its space. Marcus shares what each funding path demands, what it enables, and how to choose the one that fits your company.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Bootstrapping builds deep customer focus and culture but amplifies stress, risk aversion, and reduces real founder control
- VC funding provides capital but can distort culture; startup hype is often VC-driven marketing
- Private equity can de-risk founders and add real operational help (e.g., executive hiring, step-in support)
- Be selfish in funding choices: align capital with your vision and constraints; each path (bootstrap/VC/PE) has trade-offs and hidden incentives

—

FbvVbtvoKuY.description:
Getting to product-market fit starts with your first version. But what makes a prototype into a viable product? This session dives into how to iterate effectively, ship, and grow your business through your product from day one.

Amandine Durr, CPO at Back Market, has built products from the ground up at Dailymotion, ManoMano and AOL. From co-founding her own startup, We Are TV, to launching new lines at one of Europe’s biggest marketplaces, she shares practical lessons on turning early versions into real traction.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Product = business: tie every feature to measurable business impact and clear success metrics
- Use a rigorous hypothesis process: opportunity summary, supporting signals, opportunity sizing, and definition of success (input/output/safeguard)
- Ship MVPs to learn fast: limit scope (e.g., single market, caps) to validate hypotheses before scaling
- Embrace polarity: openly manage trade-offs (e.g., growth vs. fraud) to build decision-making and accountability
- Differentiate and narrate: double down on unique, proven features (e.g., Express Replacement) and market them with a memorable promise (“not a day without a device”)

At the dawn of every transformative era, humanity faces a pivotal moment—one that defines not just the trajectory of technology, but the future of society itself.

In the late 1800s, it was electricity. In the 1990s, it was the internet, just beginning to connect the world. If we’re drawing parallels, 2025 might well be our version of 1997: a moment when something new was in the air, but few could fully see it.

Today, that something is generative AI—and beyond it, a deeper shift we call the ground state: the new conditions that shape how everything is built.

That’s the moment we’re stepping into—and why Slush 2025 brings together:

• 6,000 startup founders and operators. 3,500 investors. Curated to the core.
• 1,000 pre-scheduled meetings per hour. Meetings that move the needle.

JguTdW8Oaao.description:
Expanding into new markets tests everything. Your culture. Your operations. Your speed. What worked in one country might fail in another. This session shows how to scale across regions while staying focused and in control.

Marina Farthouat, Chief People Officer and Chief of Staff at Oyster, draws from deep experience scaling global, remote-first teams at companies like ClickHouse and Elastic. She’ll share practical lessons on building resilient organizations across time zones, and aligning people, process, and product as you grow globally.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Build a global operating system early: clear meeting cadences, async/sync rules, and the right tooling (Slack, Notion, Loom) to drive accountability and speed.
- Prioritize culture as strategy: define behaviors to do and not do; invest in trust, recognition, and celebrating wins across borders.
- Choose a geo-based compensation strategy for fairness, transparency, and sustainable costs; communicate it early to avoid later friction.
- Design teams by function and time zones: distribute engineering; localize go-to-market; ensure overlap hours and avoid spanning the entire globe too soon.
- Incorporate local expertise and compliance support (e.g., Oyster) to reduce risk when hiring in new markets and to focus founders on growth.

- Partners are critical for global scale; leverage cloud/LLM alliances and act on today’s model quality to capture early value.

Lnv3YXd8jgo.title: Lila Tretikov: Partner @NEA, Product Differentiation, User Adoption & AI Bias | Slush 2024
Lnv3YXd8jgo.label: Slush
Lnv3YXd8jgo.description:
Lila Tretikov is a highly regarded American and French CEO, board director, entrepreneur, investor, and executive. She is a distinguished leader in Al and technology with extensive experience navigating major market disruptions fueled by technological advancements. Lila is known for top global brands as CEO and senior executive and brings a wealth of experience from founding multiple technology companies. She is renowned for her strategic foresight, customer-centric ethos, and talent for propelling exponential growth across Fortune 50 and other high-profile organizations.  In 2024, Lila joined NEA as Partner, where she oversees Al Strategy spanning over 500 portfolio companies.

In her most recent prior corporate position, Lila was Deputy CTO, CVP at Microsoft where she was instrumental in shaping Microsoft’s future growth through large-scale Al transformation. Before joining Microsoft, Lila was SVP Engie, CEO & Vice Chair Terrawatt at Engie (EPA:ENGI) where she led the company’s transition to renewable energy sources and cutting-edge technologies while the company divested from carbon-based energy sources. Previously, Lila was CEO at Wikipedia Foundation & Endowment where she reversed user and editor decline, introduced AI and multiplied revenues. Lila founded her first company while at UC Berkeley Lawrence Livermore Lab and created the first genomic browser.

Lila is recognized among Forbes’ Top 100 Most Powerful Women and honored with the prestigious designation of Young Global Leader (YGL) by the World Economic Forum.

Lila is joined on stage with Emma Hinchliffe. Emma is a senior writer at @fortune, where she covers women in business and gender issues across business, politics, and culture. Emma is the author of Most Powerful Women Daily (formerly the Broadsheet), Fortune’s daily newsletter for and about the women leading the business world. She is a co-chair of Fortune’s Most Powerful Women Summit, where she’s interviewed everyone from Fortune 500 CEOs and U.S. politicians to Hollywood stars, and previously co-chaired Fortune’s MPW Next Gen Summit and the Fortune/U.S. Department of State Global Women’s Mentoring Partnership. Her work, which includes magazine features with subjects ranging from Meta and CVS Health to Canva and the WNBA, has been honored by the Silurians Press Club. Before joining Fortune, she worked as a reporter for Mashable and the Houston Chronicle. She is a graduate of Georgetown University and lives in Brooklyn, N.Y.

Rob Snyder, Founder of Waffle and a serial entrepreneur who has lived through hard pivots and tough tradeoffs. Rob currently deadlifts 365 pounds. He’ll share real stories and practical tools for recognizing signals, avoiding false ones, and making the move with your team, customers, and investors still on board.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Pivot = evolve toward demand; follow market pull, not internal ideas
- Validate interest with payment/implementation steps (“Stripe link tells the truth”)
- Batch customer learnings in sets of five sales calls; avoid chasing every new request
- Do sales-focused conversations; observe users at work instead of generic interviews
- Bad pivots come from avoiding real sales (e.g., chasing trends/virality) and blasting cold emails instead of having conversations

Hiring can make or break your startup. So can retention. Yet most founders get their first 10 hires wrong. In this session, Elias Torres (Founder & CEO, Agency) shares lessons from building teams at Drift, HubSpot, and now Agency.

He’ll cover what actually attracts top talent, how to build loyalty without big salaries, and why culture fit matters more than you think. Expect real talk, mistakes made, and practical advice founders can use from day one.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Don’t oversell the dream: be brutally honest about stage, chaos, and expectations to self-select truly committed candidates.
- Hire slow on fit, move fast on process: validate in under 7 days without acting out of desperation.
- Test for hunger and resilience: watch for hesitation; use trials/side projects to gauge commitment.
- Avoid pedigree bias: past big-brand wins don’t guarantee impact in your context.
- Build small, elite teams in the AI era: cap headcount, prioritize versatile, high-ownership builders.

dZ0nklszeEk.label: Slush
dZ0nklszeEk.description:
Balancing product and go-to-market is one of the hardest challenges in company building. Get the timing wrong and the product might break or the market might slip away. This fireside offers rare insight into how two of the world’s fastest-moving companies approach this exact tension.

Stanley Tang, Co-Founder and Head of DoorDash Labs at DoorDash, and Niilo Säämänen, Chief Technology Officer at Wolt, share how they continue to launch ambitious new technologies while executing at scale. Using autonomy and robotics as a case study, they break down how to test bold ideas, structure small teams inside large companies, and build real feedback loops between product and GTM.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Start with the use case: define the problem first, then choose tech; avoid shiny-object R&D.
- Constrain to innovate: small, budget-limited “Labs” teams earn funding by staged proofs.
- Build systems, not silos: autonomy requires end-to-end ops (dispatch, charging, pickup/drop-off, partners).
- Ship to learn: prioritize commercialization and real-world contact to avoid “R&D hell.”
- Serendipitous wins: drone weight constraints led to Smart Scales, halving missing-item rates and aiding all deliveries.

swbfsatafBU.title: Navigating Co-founder Breakups | Paul Müller (EWOR)
swbfsatafBU.label: Slush
swbfsatafBU.description:
Co-founder breakups are a key reason why startups fail. From choosing the right partner to surviving the toughest conversations, this session unpacks what founders rarely talk about: how to prevent, navigate, and recover from co-founder breakups.

Paul Müller knows the stakes. As the founder of Adjust, which scaled from 3 to 700+ people and sold for over $1B, he’s lived the highs and lows. Now as a partner at EWOR, he shares hard-won lessons to help your startup succeed.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Choose complementary co-founders you respect intellectually; avoid 50/50 skill overlap and founding with partners/spouses.
- Align early on goals, sacrifice level, roles, decision rights, and what requires consent; define clear “turfs.”
- Put a “prenup” in place: unequal equity, long reverse vesting, and terms for role changes or underperformance.
- Watch for early signs of mismatch (ability, motivation, commitment); address it fast—don’t delay hard conversations.
- If a breakup is needed, negotiate from reality: current company value is effectively zero without founders’ commitment; structure a cash-flow-feasible exit and expect the relationship to end.

—

xRPAbz8HiDU.label: Slush
xRPAbz8HiDU.description:
Everyone celebrates wins, but almost no one talks about setbacks. Still, every startup has to face the Valley of Death.

Francesco Simoneschi, Founder & CEO of TrueLayer, shares what it feels like when things break. He speaks candidly about how to keep leading when momentum fades and belief wavers. Together with Maxine Rior, Principal at Northzone, they unpack how to hold the company together, lead through chaos, and make the hardest calls when everything is on the line.

—

AI-generated key takeaways
- Market cycles demand toolset shifts: optimize for growth when capital is cheap; pivot to monetization and efficiency when it tightens
- Act early on warning signs: public markets lead; private funding lags—overreact slightly rather than wait
- Build a high-trust core: small, aligned leadership group to make tough calls and project unity
- Communicate transparently: over-articulate strategy, admit mistakes, and guide the team through gradual change
- Use adversity as fuel: counter negative narratives with bunker mentality, focus on controllables, and prove progress with results

—
